content: Halofantrine is an antimalarial drug that acts specifically on the blood stage of the malaria parasite's life cycle. It does not exhibit any activity against the sporozoite, gametocyte, or liver stages of the infection. The precise mechanism by which halofantrine exerts its antimalarial effects remains unknown. Both the parent compound, halofantrine, and its primary metabolite, n-desbutyl halofantrine, demonstrate equivalent activity in laboratory studies. In vitro studies suggest the possibility of cross-resistance between halofantrine and mefloquine. However, clinical evidence does not support this finding, as no significant correlation between resistance to halofantrine and mefloquine was observed in clinical trials. In controlled clinical trials involving 90 non-immune patients infected with Plasmodium falciparum, treatment with Halfan (administered as 500 mg every 6 hours for three doses on days 0 and 7) achieved a cure rate of 99%. Patients were monitored for at least 28 days following the initiation of treatment. In additional trials involving 583 patients with acute malaria, most of whom were semi-immune, the same treatment regimen with Halfan resulted in a 90% cure rate for Plasmodium falciparum infections (n=512) and a 99% cure rate for Plasmodium vivax infections (n=71).
